newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan general election date still a guessing game.
newsitem.headline: Japan general election date still a guessing game.

text.p: Japan's three ruling coalition parties kept the nation guessing as to the timing of general elections by failing to announce a date for the widely anticipated polls after meeting on Thursday.

Leaders of the two minority parties considered by analysts to be against early polls emerged from talks with Prime Minister Ryutaru Hashimoto saying the timing of a general election was not discussed.

Social Democratic Party leader Tomiichi Murayama said talks with Hashimoto, the president of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), and Shoichi Ide, head of New Party Sakigake, were limited to the central government's dispute with Okinawa over the heavy concentration of U.S. military bases on the island prefecture.
"We discussed the issue of Okinawa only. There was no discussion on any possibility of a dissolution of parliament or general elections," Murayama told reporters.
Murayama echoed earlier comments by the chief government spokesman that Hashimoto was not ready to call a general election anytime soon.
"There is nothing but Okinawa on Prime Minister Hashimoto's mind," Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama told a regular news conference.

LDP Secretary-General Koichi Kato, who also attended the meeting, said Hashimoto would await a response from Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota to Tokyo's request that he force the renewal of leases for privately held land used by U.S. bases.
Ota has refused to renew the leases, despite losing a Supreme Court case last month in which he argued the state policy of forced land appropriation was unconstitutional.

A meeting on Tuesday between Hashimoto and Ota, in which the prime minister promised to shrink the bases and pump five billion yen ($45.4 million) into the Okinawan economy, raised hopes the governor would ease the year-old standoff with Tokyo.
A second Sakigake official told reporters Hashimoto did not want to offend Okinawans with electoral talk that preempted Ota's decision on the leases.
A cabinet official said the party heads would likely meet again on Friday if Tokyo received a reply from Okinawa.

Murayama and Ide, whose parties are is disarray over plans to merge prior to polls, expressed anger on Wednesday at a flurry of newspaper reports which said a general election was likely to be held on October 20.
The reports were attributed to sources in the LDP, the largest party in the ruling bloc and the party most in favour of early polls.

Hashimoto does not need to hold general elections until July 1997 and has said he would set a poll date after confirming that Japan's economy was in full recovery and after settling the Okinawa dispute.
A key economic indicator expected to influence Hashimoto's decision on polls, the April-June Gross Domestic Product data, is to be released on Friday.
Hashimoto is due to visit the United States from September 23 to 25 to hold brief talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton and to address the U.N. General Assembly. ($1-110 yen)
